stem: A company buys Reserved Instances in one account of its organization, but the matching instances run in another member account.

options.text: No; discounts only apply in the purchasing account
options.why: With consolidated billing, discounts can be shared across accounts.

options.text: Yes; RI and Savings Plans discounts can be shared across the organization
options.why: Discount sharing applies benefits across accounts by default.

options.text: Only if the accounts use the same root email
options.why: Root email has nothing to do with sharing.

options.text: Only with Enterprise Support
options.why: Support plans don't affect discount sharing.

explanation.answer: Under consolidated billing, Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts can apply to matching usage in any account in the organization.
explanation.concept: The management account can turn sharing off for specific accounts.
explanation.examTip: Discounts are shared across accounts in an organization.

references.title: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans discount sharing

stem: A company has three accounts, each storing 40 TB in S3, and they're in the same organization.
prompt: How does consolidated billing affect S3 pricing?

options.text: Each account is priced separately at its own 40 TB
options.why: With consolidated billing, usage is combined.

options.text: Each account pays a small surcharge for being a member
options.why: Consolidated billing doesn't add a surcharge.

options.text: Usage combines to 120 TB, which may reach lower tiers
options.why: Aggregated usage can qualify for volume discounts.

options.text: Organizations get S3 storage at a flat discounted rate
options.why: There's no flat organization rate; usage is combined for tiered pricing.

explanation.answer: Consolidated billing treats all accounts as one for volume pricing, so combined usage may qualify for lower tiered prices.
explanation.concept: This is one financial benefit of AWS Organizations.
explanation.examTip: Combined usage = better volume tiers.

stem: A company resells AWS to internal business units and wants to show each unit a customized bill with its own pricing rates.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
options.why: This estimates costs for planned workloads.

options.text: AWS Budgets
options.why: Budgets track spending against limits, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: AWS Billing Conductor
options.why: Billing Conductor creates customized pro forma billing data with custom rates.

explanation.answer: AWS Billing Conductor lets you customize billing data for showback and chargeback, with custom pricing rules and groups of accounts.
explanation.concept: It doesn't change what you pay AWS; it changes how costs are presented.
explanation.examTip: Custom showback/chargeback bills = Billing Conductor.

stem: A finance team wants to group costs into business-level categories, such as "Marketing" or "Platform", using rules based on accounts and tags.

options.text: AWS Cost Categories
options.why: Cost Categories map costs into custom groups using rules.

options.text: Security groups
options.why: Security groups filter traffic, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Amazon Route 53
options.why: Route 53 is DNS, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: AWS Snowball Edge
options.why: Snowball moves data, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: AWS Cost Categories let you create rules that group costs by accounts, tags, services and more, for reports and budgets.
explanation.concept: They appear in Cost Explorer, Budgets and the Cost and Usage Report.
explanation.examTip: Business-level cost groups = Cost Categories.

references.title: Organizing costs using AWS Cost Categories

stem: A company deleted its EC2 instances but keeps paying for storage.
prompt: What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The Management Console charges for logins
options.why: The console is free, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Unattached EBS volumes or old snapshots still exist
options.why: EBS volumes and snapshots are billed until deleted.

options.text: IAM users are billed monthly
options.why: IAM has no charge, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Terminated instances are billed for 30 days
options.why: Terminated instances stop billing, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: EBS volumes are billed for provisioned storage whether or not they're attached. Snapshots are billed for stored data.
explanation.concept: Check for unattached volumes and old snapshots regularly.
explanation.examTip: Paying for storage after deleting instances = leftover EBS volumes/snapshots.

stem: A company notices a charge for public IPv4 addresses on its bill.

options.text: Only unused Elastic IPs are charged, and only in us-east-1
options.why: Charges apply across Regions and to in-use addresses too.

options.text: Public IPv4 addresses are free while attached to an instance
options.why: AWS charges for public IPv4 addresses whether they're attached or idle.

options.text: AWS charges hourly for public IPv4 addresses, whether in use or not
options.why: Public IPv4 addresses, including Elastic IPs, are billed per hour.

options.text: IPv6 addresses are charged more than IPv4
options.why: IPv6 addresses aren't charged this way, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: AWS charges for all public IPv4 addresses, in use or idle, on an hourly basis.
explanation.concept: Using IPv6 or private addressing can reduce these charges.
explanation.examTip: Public IPv4 = hourly charge.

stem: A company wants to automatically stop new EC2 launches in a sandbox account when its monthly budget is exceeded.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
options.why: Cost Anomaly Detection alerts on unusual spend but doesn't restrict launches.

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
options.why: This estimates planned costs, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: AWS Budgets actions
options.why: Budget actions can apply IAM policies or SCPs, or stop instances, when thresholds are crossed.

explanation.answer: AWS Budgets actions run automatically when a budget threshold is exceeded, such as applying an IAM policy or SCP to restrict usage.
explanation.concept: This adds enforcement on top of alerts.
explanation.examTip: Auto-restrict when over budget = Budgets actions.

stem: A company asks which of these AWS features has no additional charge.
prompt: Which is offered at no additional charge?

options.text: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)
options.why: IAM is offered at no additional charge, which matches what the question asks for.

options.text: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts
options.why: Dedicated Hosts are physical servers billed by the hour.

options.text: AWS Shield Advanced
options.why: Shield Advanced is a paid subscription, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Amazon S3 storage beyond the Free Tier
options.why: S3 storage is billed per GB, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: IAM, AWS Organizations, consolidated billing and the Management Console are offered at no additional charge.
explanation.concept: Resources you create with these tools are billed normally.
explanation.examTip: Free features: IAM, Organizations, consolidated billing, console.

stem: A company wants AWS to recommend how much to commit to Savings Plans based on its past usage.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer
options.why: Cost Explorer provides Savings Plans and RI purchase recommendations.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
options.why: This estimates planned costs, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: AWS Cost Explorer analyzes your usage and recommends Savings Plans and Reserved Instance purchases, with estimated savings.
explanation.concept: It also shows utilization and coverage of existing commitments.
explanation.examTip: Commitment recommendations = Cost Explorer.

stem: A company's application constantly sends large amounts of data between instances in different Availability Zones.
prompt: What should it know about the cost?

options.text: Only data transfer within one AZ is charged
options.why: Same-AZ traffic over private IPs is generally free.

options.text: Inter-AZ data transfer is charged only with Enterprise Support
options.why: Support plans don't affect data transfer pricing.

options.text: Data transfer between AZs is charged per GB in each direction
options.why: Inter-AZ traffic is billed, so chatty cross-AZ designs can add cost.

options.text: Data transfer between AZs in one Region is free
options.why: Data transfer between AZs is generally charged per GB.

explanation.answer: Data transferred between Availability Zones in the same Region is charged per GB. Data within the same AZ over private IP is generally free.
explanation.concept: Balance resilience (multi-AZ) with data transfer costs.
explanation.examTip: Cross-AZ traffic costs money; same-AZ private traffic usually doesn't.

stem: A company is setting up AWS Organizations for billing.
prompt: Which TWO are benefits of consolidated billing? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Free EC2 instances in member accounts
options.why: Consolidated billing doesn't make resources free.

options.text: Automatic removal of unused resources
options.why: Billing features don't delete resources.

options.text: Combined usage for volume pricing tiers
options.why: Aggregated usage can reach lower price tiers.

options.text: One bill for multiple accounts
options.why: Consolidated billing produces a single bill.

options.text: Unlimited AWS Support at no charge
options.why: Support plans are billed separately, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: Consolidated billing gives one bill, combined usage for volume discounts, and sharing of RI and Savings Plans discounts.
explanation.concept: It's included with AWS Organizations at no additional charge.
explanation.examTip: Consolidated billing = one bill + volume tiers + shared discounts.

stem: A company asks what it pays for with Amazon DynamoDB on-demand mode.

options.text: Only data transfer into DynamoDB
options.why: Data in is not the main driver, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Only the number of tables
options.why: Table count isn't the main cost driver, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: A fixed hourly fee per table
options.why: On-demand isn't billed as a fixed fee per table.

options.text: Read and write requests plus data stored
options.why: On-demand charges per request and for storage.

explanation.answer: DynamoDB on-demand charges for read and write request units used and for data storage, plus optional features.
explanation.concept: Provisioned mode charges for capacity units per hour.
explanation.examTip: DynamoDB on-demand = per request + storage.

stem: A company runs a production web server that must stay up but tries to save money with Spot Instances.

options.text: AWS can reclaim Spot capacity with a two-minute warning
options.why: Interruptions can take the web server down if it isn't designed for them.

options.text: Spot Instances can't run Linux
options.why: Spot supports Linux and Windows, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Spot Instances can't use EBS volumes
options.why: Spot instances can use EBS, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Spot Instances cost more than On-Demand
options.why: Spot is cheaper, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: Spot Instances can be interrupted when AWS needs the capacity back, with a two-minute notice.
explanation.concept: Use Spot for fault-tolerant parts of workloads, or mix it with On-Demand in Auto Scaling groups.
explanation.examTip: Spot = cheap but can be interrupted.

stem: A developer wants the official price per hour for a specific RDS instance type in a specific Region.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
options.why: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: The service's pricing page or the AWS Price List API
options.why: Pricing pages and the Price List API publish current prices by Region.

options.text: The AWS Cost and Usage Report for last month
options.why: The CUR shows what you were billed, not list prices for instance types you haven't used.

options.text: AWS Artifact pricing reports for each service
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: Each AWS service has a pricing page with prices by Region. The AWS Price List API provides prices programmatically.
explanation.concept: Prices can differ between Regions.
explanation.examTip: Exact price = service pricing page / Price List API.

stem: A company wants every new resource to carry a "CostCenter" tag so costs can be attributed.
prompt: Which feature helps enforce consistent tags across accounts?

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
options.why: This estimates costs, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: AWS Config conformance packs
options.why: Config can check for tags, but tag policies standardize tag keys and values across accounts.

options.text: Tag policies in AWS Organizations
options.why: Tag policies standardize tag keys and values across accounts.

options.text: S3 Lifecycle rules
options.why: Lifecycle rules manage objects, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: Tag policies in AWS Organizations help standardize tags across accounts. SCPs can deny resource creation without required tags.
explanation.concept: Consistent tagging is the foundation of cost allocation.
explanation.examTip: Standardize tags across accounts = Organizations tag policies.

stem: A company asks why it might buy software through AWS Marketplace instead of directly from vendors.

options.text: All Marketplace software is free
options.why: Many products are paid, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Marketplace replaces the need for security controls
options.why: Customers still secure their deployments.

options.text: Marketplace products are maintained by AWS
options.why: Third-party sellers maintain their products.

options.text: Charges appear on the AWS bill and products deploy quickly to AWS
options.why: Marketplace simplifies procurement and deployment.

explanation.answer: AWS Marketplace simplifies buying, deploying and paying for third-party software, with billing through your AWS account.
explanation.concept: Private offers allow negotiated pricing.
explanation.examTip: Marketplace = buy third-party software, pay on AWS bill.

stem: A company has a Compute Savings Plan and starts running AWS Fargate tasks and Lambda functions.
prompt: How is the new usage billed?

options.text: The discount can apply to Fargate and Lambda usage too
options.why: Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda.

options.text: At a separate Fargate and Lambda Savings Plan rate
options.why: No separate plan is needed; Compute Savings Plans already apply.

options.text: The plan is paused until the next billing month
options.why: Plans aren't paused by using other services.

options.text: At On-Demand rates, because Savings Plans cover EC2 only
options.why: Compute Savings Plans also cover Fargate and Lambda.

explanation.answer: Compute Savings Plans apply automatically to eligible usage across EC2, AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda, up to the hourly commitment.
explanation.concept: Usage above the commitment is billed at On-Demand rates.
explanation.examTip: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2 + Fargate + Lambda.

stem: A company on Basic Support has a question about why its EC2 application is slow.

options.text: Request a review from a designated TAM this week
options.why: TAMs require Enterprise Support, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Use documentation, re:Post and core checks, or upgrade
options.why: Basic covers self-service resources; technical cases need a paid plan.

options.text: Open a technical support case by phone with an engineer
options.why: Basic doesn't include technical support cases.

options.text: Ask the Concierge Support Team to troubleshoot it
options.why: Concierge comes with Enterprise-level plans.

explanation.answer: Basic Support provides account and billing help and self-service resources. Technical support cases require Developer or higher.
explanation.concept: Upgrading can be done anytime in the console.
explanation.examTip: Technical question on Basic = self-service or upgrade.

stem: A finance team is choosing cost tools.
prompt: Which TWO pairings are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor – pay invoices
options.why: Invoices are paid in the Billing console.

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer – estimate costs before creating an account
options.why: Cost Explorer analyzes actual usage in an account.

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator – estimate a planned architecture
options.why: The calculator estimates future costs, so it meets the requirement described here.

options.text: AWS Budgets – alert when spending exceeds a threshold
options.why: Budgets sends alerts on thresholds, so it meets the requirement described here.

options.text: AWS Artifact – show spend by service
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Pricing Calculator = estimate. Cost Explorer = analyze actual spend. Budgets = alert. CUR = detailed data.
explanation.concept: These four tools appear often on the exam.
explanation.examTip: Estimate=Calculator, analyze=Cost Explorer, alert=Budgets, details=CUR.

stem: A company is reviewing its AWS bill to understand the fundamental cost drivers.
prompt: Which are the three fundamental drivers of AWS cost?

options.text: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations
options.why: These are infrastructure concepts, not cost drivers by themselves.

options.text: Support cases, Trusted Advisor checks and tags
options.why: These aren't the fundamental drivers, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Compute, storage and outbound data transfer
options.why: These are the three fundamental drivers of AWS costs.

options.text: Users, passwords and policies
options.why: IAM is free and doesn't drive cost, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: AWS describes three fundamental cost drivers: compute, storage and outbound data transfer.
explanation.concept: Most service pricing combines these drivers.
explanation.examTip: Cost drivers = compute + storage + data out.
